hero.title: Designing future computing hardware with new technologies, circuits, and architectures
hero.lead: NEXUS — Nanoelectronics EXpeditions for Ubiquitous Systems — explores cross-stack advances in semiconductor technologies, heterogeneous integration, circuit design, and computer architecture for large improvements in computing energy efficiency and throughput.

about.title: Hardware systems for an abundant-data world
paragraphs: The NEXUS Research Group is focused on advancing the field of hardware systems to support the growing computational needs of today's abundant-data applications. Large language models, edge AI, and scientific computing are demanding orders of magnitude more compute than traditional transistor miniaturization can deliver.

We attack that gap across the whole stack at once. New nanoelectronic devices, dense three-dimensional integration, co-designed circuits, and domain-specific architectures are far more powerful together than any of them is alone — so we build the tools, the silicon, and the design methodologies that let them be designed together.

The group is led by Dr. Tathagata Srimani in the Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering at Carnegie Mellon University, and works closely with collaborators across academia, national labs, and industry foundries.
highlights: First CNFET-based RISC-V microprocessor and first CNFET + CMOS monolithic-3D system, transitioned to industrial fabrication
Symbolic co-design frameworks that derive technology targets from application-level performance goals
Probabilistic computing ASICs for NP-hard optimization problems

research.title: Three thrusts, one stack
research.lead: Our work spans emerging devices to full systems. Each thrust below feeds the others — technology informs architecture, and architecture sets the targets technology has to hit.

areas.title: 3D Integration
areas.summary: Advancing technology and circuits for next-generation 3D-integrated computing systems.
body: Modern applications spend an outsized share of their time and energy simply moving data between logic and memory — the memory wall — without doing useful computation. 3D integration attacks this on two fronts: vertical stacking increases logic and memory capacity within the same footprint, and fine-grained vertical connections such as monolithic 3D integration or hybrid bonding raise bandwidth and cut latency between compute and memory.

We develop monolithic 3D systems that combine high-performance logic with dense, low-energy memory in stacked tiers, including carbon nanotube FETs (CNFETs) for performance at low voltages alongside 3D resistive RAM (RRAM). These architectures substantially reduce data-movement overhead and improve energy-delay for AI accelerators relative to conventional 2D systems.

As stacking scales, thermal management and power delivery become the binding constraints. We co-design high-thermal-conductivity back-end-of-line dielectrics with optimized power delivery networks so that multiple high-power 3D compute tiers can actually be built.

areas.title: Technology–Architecture Co-Design
areas.summary: Frameworks that link application performance requirements to hardware and technology targets.
body: We build frameworks for co-designing technologies and architectures with two objectives: quick estimation of application performance — written in a high-level language — for given technology parameters across logic, memory, and on-chip/inter-chip connectivity; and derivation of technology targets from application performance needs such as energy and execution time, including for future, yet-to-be-discovered technologies.

Our symbolic co-design methodology captures dependencies between applications, architectures, and technologies. A forward pass optimizes architectural designs for a fixed technology; an inverse pass derives the technology parameters a target workload would require. PyTorch models feed high-level synthesis toolchains to generate dataflow graphs, followed by physical design analysis for interconnect parasitics and energy-delay modeling.

On the interconnect side, we progress from conventional 2D crossbar arrays to folded 2D network-on-chip designs and finally to 3D-optimized topologies that exploit ultra-dense inter-layer vias below 100 nm for far greater bandwidth.

areas.title: Domain-Specific Accelerators
areas.summary: Specialized hardware for compute- and data-intensive workloads that general-purpose accelerators handle poorly.
body: Classical accelerators like GPUs and TPUs are optimized for deterministic algorithms and struggle with probabilistic tasks such as Monte Carlo and Markov Chain Monte Carlo. We build domain-specific probabilistic computing hardware to address those scaling challenges, using probabilistic bits (p-bits) — classical bits that fluctuate between states probabilistically — as the fundamental computing element rather than quantum systems.
Chimera is an area-optimized reconfigurable accelerator with a novel topology, supporting up to 16,384 spins with 10-bit coefficient precision in just 0.5 mm² of core area at 17.09 µW per spin.

Pegasus is a scalable digital Ising machine on a different graph topology, supporting dense connectivity and multi-chip scalability through asynchronous communication, with 6,192 time-multiplexed nodes running at 200 MHz — a CMOS-compatible route to NP-hard optimization.

courses.title: Hacker Fab
courses.description: An open-source micro- and nanofabrication facility where students collaborate to design and build state-of-the-art process equipment, with a focus on semiconductor device fabrication and emerging technologies.

courses.title: Advanced Digital Integrated Circuit Design
courses.description: Student teams create a moderate-sized digital, analog/RF, or mixed-signal chip in a modern technology using industrial CAD tools and flows, culminating in designs sent out for fabrication.
